clue.text: Copper's going back into wood, as it is described

indicators.note: going back means the letters run in the opposite direction
into tells us one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: ash is a timber tree
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper, plus the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: A policeman retreating into the woods, reported exactly as it happened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman but is the metal, Cu. Its reversal sits inside the tree to give AS SUCH.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'as such' means in the strict sense, in the capacity described.

clue.text: Worker admits knowing one's a bolshevik

indicators.note: something that admits lets others in, so it holds them inside

blocks.note: a worker ant is the classic crossword worker
arch means knowing or sly, as in an arch look
one is I, and 's is read as is

explanation.surface: An employee lets slip that he is a revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: A worker is an ant by crossword convention. The lower-case bolshevik is used loosely for any revolutionary agitator.
explanation.definitionFit: A bolshevik in the loose sense is a radical revolutionary, much like someone who rejects all government.

clue.text: Navigator sinks, carried far out

indicators.note: out suggests things are wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A seafarer's ship goes down, swept far out to sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Francis Drake was the Elizabethan seaman who sailed around the globe, a celebrated navigator.

clue.text: Dispense with popular composer

blocks.note: to chop something is to cut it, get rid of it
what is in is fashionable

explanation.surface: An instruction to drop a well-liked composer from the programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Frédéric Chopin was the Polish Romantic who wrote mainly piano music.

clue.text: Improves looks at college

blocks.note: shapes are forms or outward looks
up means in residence at university

explanation.surface: A student's appearance gets better once at university.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage you are 'up' at Oxford or Cambridge while studying there.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who shapes up gets their act together and performs better.

clue.text: Vehicle to reverse after clutch employed

blocks.note: a clutch of eggs is a hatch, a brood
to back a car is to reverse it

explanation.surface: A driver uses the clutch to reverse the car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clutch' is a car pedal in the surface but a brood of eggs in the wordplay; 'after' puts BACK behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatchback is a car type with a rear door that lifts up.

clue.text: Difficulties learner found in examination paper initially

indicators.note: found in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: a probe is an investigation
MS, the initials of manuscript, is a written paper
L is the learner-driver plate

explanation.surface: A student struggles at the start of an exam paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' marks the abbreviation of manuscript, a written paper, formed from its initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Problems are troubles or hard matters to resolve, the same as difficulties.

clue.text: Dangle weights in at sea (old nautical term)

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sailor lowers weighted lines into the water to sound the depth.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface itself describes the original practice: sounding depth with a lead weight on a line, a job sailors could spin out to avoid harder work.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for shirking originated on ships, where heaving a lead line was an easy task, so it is a seafaring expression.

clue.text: Heathen opening up before article appears

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a gap is an opening
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A non-believer turns up first and then a newspaper piece appears.
explanation.definitionFit: A pagan follows a non-mainstream or polytheistic religion, historically called a heathen.

clue.text: Blue-eyed boy: not working, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly signals that we go by how a word is spoken

blocks.note: idle means not working

explanation.surface: The favourite son is said to be lazy.
explanation.walkthrough: A blue-eyed boy is British slang for a favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is an adored favourite, just as the blue-eyed boy is the one everybody dotes on.

clue.text: Icing in tandoori? Unlikely tandoori may have it

indicators.note: unlikely suggests an improbable arrangement, so the letters are reshuffled

blocks.note: the fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Nobody puts icing on tandoori chicken, but the hot restaurant might well be cooled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tandoori' does double duty: in the definition it is an Indian restaurant, which might be air-conditioned.
explanation.definitionFit: A tandoori restaurant, with its hot ovens, may well have cooling equipment installed.

clue.text: Warm and stimulating drink

blocks.note: first meaning: friendly, sincere
second meaning: a fruit drink or reviving liqueur

explanation.surface: A description of a hot, invigorating beverage.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means friendly and also names a sweet drink once taken as a heart tonic.

clue.text: Henry has information about oxygen and iodine, perhaps

blocks.note: Hal is a pet name for Henry, as in Shakespeare's Prince Hal
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
gen is British slang for information; it comes about, round behind, the oxygen

explanation.surface: Henry is briefed on the chemistry of two elements.
explanation.walkthrough: HAL, O and GEN join up. Iodine is a halogen but oxygen is not, which is why only iodine is the example.
explanation.definitionFit: Iodine belongs to the group of reactive elements alongside fluorine, chlorine and bromine; 'perhaps' marks it as one example.

clue.text: Girl heading off for a Hebridean island

indicators.note: heading off says the first letter is removed

blocks.note: a girl's name

explanation.surface: A young woman sets off on a trip to the Scottish isles.
explanation.definitionFit: Iona is a small island in the Inner Hebrides off Mull, famous for its abbey.

clue.text: Einstein and Wittgenstein are of the same opinion, or so the saying goes?

definitions.text: Einstein and Wittgenstein are of the same opinion, or so the saying goes?

blocks.clueFragment: Einstein and Wittgenstein are of the same opinion
blocks.note: surface reading: two famous thinkers happen to agree
setter's reading: a proverb that is said whenever two people share an idea

explanation.surface: Two celebrated intellectuals find themselves agreeing.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is normally said when two ordinary people hit on the same idea; here it is applied literally to two real geniuses.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb fits exactly: two brilliant thinkers agreeing are its literal case.

clue.text: They make for a bigger pool as waves engulf central part of cove

definitions.text: They make for a bigger pool

indicators.note: central part of keeps only the middle letters
to engulf is to swallow up and surround

blocks.note: rollers are long heavy waves
the two middle letters of cove

explanation.surface: Waves sweep into a cove and make the swimming pool larger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pool' is not water but a lottery jackpot: unwon prizes roll over.
explanation.definitionFit: When nobody wins a lottery, the prize money carries over to the next draw and the jackpot grows.

clue.text: Notice fixed right inside loose one

indicators.note: loose suggests something come apart and free to move around
inside places one piece within another

blocks.note: set means fixed in place
taken as written, to be rearranged
'right!' is an expression of agreement

explanation.surface: Spot that a fixing has come loose inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right' is not R here but a word of agreement, as in 'Right, let's go'.
explanation.definitionFit: To set eyes on someone is to catch sight of them, to spot or observe them.

clue.text: Smallest bones?

definitions.note: adjective, as in a skeleton staff

blocks.note: first meaning: reduced to the minimum
second meaning: the framework of the body

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a question about the tiniest bones in the body; really it is two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the bony frame of a body and, attributively, a bare-minimum service or staff.

clue.text: See 14
A small songbird occupied in a particular way

blocks.note: taken as written
a tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: A little bird busy with its own particular activity.
explanation.definitionFit: To be 'at it' is to be busy, engaged in some activity, often one hinted at.

clue.text: See game bird in Greek river

blocks.note: Gr is the abbreviation for Greek
the Ouse is an English river

explanation.surface: An instruction to look at a game bird by a river in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is the solver's instruction, as in a cross-reference. The Ouse is a river in Yorkshire, and another in East Anglia.
explanation.definitionFit: The grouse is a plump moorland bird shot for sport in Britain.

clue.text: Nobleman, one pleased to be backed in House

indicators.note: backed means put into reverse
in places these pieces inside another

blocks.note: Ho is the abbreviation for house
the Roman numeral for one
glad means pleased

explanation.surface: An aristocrat is delighted to have support in the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the word for pleased is turned round; the numeral stays in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidalgo is a Spanish gentleman of the lower nobility.

clue.text: Birds of prey - last of such birds, we're told

indicators.note: last of keeps only the final letter
we're told points to something heard rather than read

blocks.note: the final letter of such
auks are seabirds such as the guillemot

explanation.surface: Raptors, apparently the final word in such birds.
explanation.walkthrough: H plus a sound-alike of AUKS. Auks are northern seabirds; the great auk is extinct.
explanation.definitionFit: Hawks are raptors that hunt other animals, the common example of predatory birds.

clue.text: Copy in smithy by railway

blocks.note: a forge is a blacksmith's workshop
Ry is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A duplicate made in the blacksmith's shop by the railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copy' as a verb in the surface becomes a noun for a fake.
explanation.definitionFit: A forgery is a fraudulent imitation of a document or artwork.

clue.text: Plant found in bogland bordering river

indicators.note: bordering means lying on both sides, enclosing

blocks.note: a fen is marshy ground
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A plant growing in a marsh beside a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A fern is a flowerless green plant reproducing by spores.

clue.text: Take charge as stormy weather approaches vulnerable US resort

indicators.note: stormy suggests turbulence, so the letters are tossed about
vulnerable suggests something that can be broken up and reshaped

blocks.note: the first set of letters to rearrange
the second set of letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone takes command as a hurricane heads for an exposed American beach town.
explanation.definitionFit: To wear the trousers is the idiom for being the dominant partner who makes the decisions.

clue.text: Most demanding Irish novelist stumped

blocks.note: Laurence Sterne, born in Ireland, wrote Tristram Shandy
st is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for stumped

explanation.surface: The most exacting Irish writer is lost for words.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman is stumped when the wicketkeeper breaks the wicket while he is out of his ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Sternest is the superlative of stern, meaning strict and exacting.

clue.text: Oppressive, the French port

blocks.note: le is French for the
Aden is a port in Yemen

explanation.surface: A French port is described as stifling.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaden skies or air are heavy and dull, weighing down like lead.
